items.stem: Describe the global distribution of earthquakes.
items.answer: Narrow belts along plate boundaries: around the Pacific Ring of Fire, along the Alpine-Himalayan belt, along mid-ocean ridges; shallow at ridges and transform faults, deep at subduction zones; few within plates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point with example [4]

items.stem: Explain why volcanic eruptions at destructive boundaries are more hazardous than those at constructive boundaries.
items.answer: Andesitic and rhyolitic magma is viscous and gas-rich, so eruptions are explosive with pyroclastic flows, ash and lahars; constructive-boundary basaltic eruptions are effusive with lava flows; destructive boundaries are often densely populated.

items.stem: Table 9.1 classifies the 97 earthquakes of magnitude 7.0 or more recorded in a period by tectonic setting: subduction (destructive) boundaries 69, collision boundaries 17, constructive boundaries 3, transform boundaries 4, intraplate locations 4. Explain why earthquakes at constructive boundaries are usually small and shallow.
items.answer: The crust is thin and hot, so it cannot store much strain; faults are short and normal faulting releases stress frequently.

items.answer: (a) 235° (b) Stress builds where the plates lock along a large, gently dipping fault (megathrust); the rupture area is very large, so the energy released is great; the Benioff zone extends deep.

items.stem: Mateo argues that the type of plate boundary is the main factor determining the hazards produced by tectonic activity. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to magma type, vulnerability and secondary hazards.
items.answer: For: Boundary type controls magma type and eruption style, earthquake depth and magnitude (megathrust earthquakes and tsunamis at subduction zones). Against: Hazard impacts also depend on local geology (liquefaction in Mexico City), population density, building quality, preparedness and secondary hazards; hotspots produce hazards away from boundaries. Conclusion: Boundary type explains the nature of the physical hazard, but the effects on people depend on vulnerability.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “Pacific Ring of Fire”?
options: The belt of subduction zones around the Pacific Ocean containing about 75% of the world’s active volcanoes and most large earthquakes.
The inclined zone of earthquake foci along a subducting plate.
A fixed plume of hot mantle material that produces volcanoes within a plate, such as Hawaii.
A convergent boundary where denser oceanic lithosphere sinks beneath another plate.
items.answer: The belt of subduction zones around the Pacific Ocean containing about 75% of the world’s active volcanoes and most large earthquakes.

items.answer: Not correct. Intraplate earthquakes occur on old faults, e.g. New Madrid (USA) in 1811-12.

items.stem: Explain the occurrence of volcanoes away from plate boundaries.
items.answer: Mantle plumes create hotspots under plates; as the plate moves over the fixed hotspot, a chain of volcanoes forms, e.g. the Hawaiian-Emperor chain.

items.stem: Explain how liquefaction occurs and why it is hazardous.
items.answer: Shaking increases pore-water pressure in saturated sands and silts, so grains lose contact and the soil behaves like a liquid; buildings tilt or sink, pipes break, sand boils erupt (Christchurch 2011, Kobe port 1995).

items.stem: Explain the formation of a tsunami and why its height increases near the coast.
items.answer: Sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor at a subduction zone displaces the water column; waves spread out with long wavelengths and high speed; in shallow water they slow, wavelength shortens and height increases (shoaling).

items.stem: Two earthquakes occurred in a subduction zone: earthquake X of magnitude 6.9 and earthquake Y of magnitude 8.4. Earthquake Y generated a tsunami in water about 4 500 m deep. Tsunami speed v = √(gd), where g = 9.81 m/s² and d is the depth in metres. A coastal town lies 400 km from the epicentre. Explain why the tsunami wave height increases as it approaches the coast.
items.answer: In shallower water the wave slows; the energy is compressed into a shorter wavelength, so the height increases (shoaling); bays and estuaries can funnel it further.

items.answer: (a) 32 times (b) In shallower water the wave slows; the energy is compressed into a shorter wavelength, so the height increases (shoaling); bays and estuaries can funnel it further.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that secondary hazards cause more deaths than primary hazards in earthquakes? In your answer you may refer to tsunami and vulnerability.
items.answer: For: Tsunamis (2004 Indian Ocean, about 230 000 deaths; 2011 Tōhoku), landslides (2008 Sichuan), fires (1923 Kantō) and disease can cause most deaths. Against: Building collapse from ground shaking causes most deaths in many earthquakes (Haiti 2010, Turkey-Syria 2023 with over 50 000 deaths); vulnerability is the key factor. Conclusion: It depends on setting: subduction earthquakes near coasts are dominated by tsunamis, but in most earthquakes building collapse from shaking is the main killer.

items.stem: Explain why pyroclastic flows are the most dangerous volcanic hazard.
items.answer: They move at over 100 km/h at temperatures of several hundred °C, so escape is impossible; they burn, bury and asphyxiate everything in their path (St Pierre 1902, Merapi 2010).

items.stem: Explain how lahars form and why they can affect places far from the volcano.
items.answer: Ash mixes with water from heavy rain, melted ice or crater lakes; the mudflow follows river valleys at high speed for tens of kilometres, burying towns downstream (Armero, 74 km from Ruiz).

items.stem: An eruption of a volcano in the Philippines produced about 0.05 km³ of tephra. items.answer: Acoustic flow monitors upstream linked to sirens; hazard mapping and relocation; check dams (sabo dams) and channels; evacuation drills.

items.stem: “Volcanic hazards have greater impacts than earthquake hazards.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to deaths and prediction.
items.answer: For: Large eruptions affect wide areas and global climate (Tambora 1815, the “year without a summer”); pyroclastic flows and lahars are deadly; ash disrupts aviation. Against: Earthquakes strike without warning and have caused far more deaths in recent decades (Haiti 2010, 2004 tsunami, Turkey-Syria 2023); volcanoes can be monitored and evacuated (Pinatubo 1991). Conclusion: Earthquakes usually have greater impacts on people because they are hard to predict, though the largest eruptions can have global effects.

items.stem: Explain how the effects of volcanic eruptions can be global.
items.answer: Large eruptions inject sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere, forming aerosols that reflect sunlight and cool global temperatures (Pinatubo cooled the world by about 0.5 °C); ash clouds disrupt aviation (Eyjafjallajökull 2010).

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Lahars can occur years after an eruption.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Rain remobilises ash deposits, as around Pinatubo for years after 1991.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why pyroclastic flows are the most dangerous volcanic hazard. (b) Explain how lahars form and why they can affect places far from the volcano.
items.answer: (a) They move at over 100 km/h at temperatures of several hundred °C, so escape is impossible; they burn, bury and asphyxiate everything in their path (St Pierre 1902, Merapi 2010). (b) Ash mixes with water from heavy rain, melted ice or crater lakes; the mudflow follows river valleys at high speed for tens of kilometres, burying towns downstream (Armero, 74 km from Ruiz).

items.stem: An eruption of a stratovolcano in the Andes produced about 0.02 km³ of tephra. items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that volcanic hazards have greater impacts than earthquake hazards.
items.answer: For: Large eruptions affect wide areas and global climate (Tambora 1815, the “year without a summer”); pyroclastic flows and lahars are deadly; ash disrupts aviation. Against: Earthquakes strike without warning and have caused far more deaths in recent decades (Haiti 2010, 2004 tsunami, Turkey-Syria 2023); volcanoes can be monitored and evacuated (Pinatubo 1991). Conclusion: Earthquakes usually have greater impacts on people because they are hard to predict, though the largest eruptions can have global effects.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “All earthquakes occur at plate boundaries.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A revision website states: “Shield volcanoes are typical of subduction zones.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Intraplate earthquakes occur on old faults, e.g. New Madrid (USA) in 1811-12. (b) Not correct. Shield volcanoes form from runny basalt at hotspots and ridges; composite cones are typical of subduction zones.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Describe the global distribution of earthquakes. (b) Explain why volcanic eruptions at destructive boundaries are more hazardous than those at constructive boundaries.
items.answer: (a) Narrow belts along plate boundaries: around the Pacific Ring of Fire, along the Alpine-Himalayan belt, along mid-ocean ridges; shallow at ridges and transform faults, deep at subduction zones; few within plates. (b) Andesitic and rhyolitic magma is viscous and gas-rich, so eruptions are explosive with pyroclastic flows, ash and lahars; constructive-boundary basaltic eruptions are effusive with lava flows; destructive boundaries are often densely populated.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point with example [4] (b) [4]

items.stem: Table 9.1 classifies the 78 earthquakes of magnitude 7.0 or more recorded in a period by tectonic setting: subduction (destructive) boundaries 55, collision boundaries 8, constructive boundaries 3, transform boundaries 9, intraplate locations 3. Explain why earthquakes at constructive boundaries are usually small and shallow.
items.answer: The crust is thin and hot, so it cannot store much strain; faults are short and normal faulting releases stress frequently.

items.stem: Table 9.1 classifies the 87 earthquakes of magnitude 7.0 or more recorded in a period by tectonic setting: subduction (destructive) boundaries 58, collision boundaries 13, constructive boundaries 6, transform boundaries 7, intraplate locations 3. items.answer: Buildings are not designed for earthquakes, people are unprepared, and old cold crust transmits shaking over large distances.

items.stem: “The type of plate boundary is the main factor determining the hazards produced by tectonic activity.” How far do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: Boundary type controls magma type and eruption style, earthquake depth and magnitude (megathrust earthquakes and tsunamis at subduction zones). Against: Hazard impacts also depend on local geology (liquefaction in Mexico City), population density, building quality, preparedness and secondary hazards; hotspots produce hazards away from boundaries. Conclusion: Boundary type explains the nature of the physical hazard, but the effects on people depend on vulnerability.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A student writes: “Magnitude and intensity measure the same thing.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the formation of a tsunami and why its height increases near the coast.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Magnitude measures energy released; intensity measures the effects at a place. (b) Sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor at a subduction zone displaces the water column; waves spread out with long wavelengths and high speed; in shallow water they slow, wavelength shortens and height increases (shoaling).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) [4]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the formation of a tsunami and why its height increases near the coast. (b) Explain how liquefaction occurs and why it is hazardous.
items.answer: (a) Sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor at a subduction zone displaces the water column; waves spread out with long wavelengths and high speed; in shallow water they slow, wavelength shortens and height increases (shoaling). (b) Shaking increases pore-water pressure in saturated sands and silts, so grains lose contact and the soil behaves like a liquid; buildings tilt or sink, pipes break, sand boils erupt (Christchurch 2011, Kobe port 1995).

items.stem: Two earthquakes occurred in a subduction zone: earthquake X of magnitude 6 and earthquake Y of magnitude 8.5. Earthquake Y generated a tsunami in water about 4 000 m deep. Tsunami speed v = √(gd), where g = 9.81 m/s² and d is the depth in metres. A coastal town lies 800 km from the epicentre. Explain why the tsunami wave height increases as it approaches the coast.
items.answer: In shallower water the wave slows; the energy is compressed into a shorter wavelength, so the height increases (shoaling); bays and estuaries can funnel it further.
